title: Technical deep dive — guardrails & moderation performance impact
summary: Deep technical discussion about where to place safety filters and moderation to minimize latency/throughput impact. Covered inline vs async moderation, cost/throughput tradeoffs, KV cache and batching interactions, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem options for customer-controlled moderation. Agreed to run targeted benchmarks and share security/compliance docs.
topics: moderation model overhead (latency per request, per-token costs)
action_items: Ava: run latency+throughput benchmark comparing inline (sync) moderation vs async pipeline with 100 concurrent RPS by 2025-03-14
Samir: share Redwood moderation architecture doc, SOC2 summary, and link to safety tuning guide by 2025-03-10
Carlos: provide 10 representative prompt sets (edge cases + production) and expected signal categories by 2025-03-12
Priya: confirm whether customer requires on-prem moderation or VPC-hosted, and list compliance constraints by 2025-03-11
next_steps: Send security/compliance pack and architecture diagram (Samir)
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark outcomes and pilot plan (tentative week of 2025-03-17)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-07 15:00 UTC | Duration: 75 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ava Liu (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Acme, Lead ML Eng), Priya Kapoor (Acme, Security Architect), Liam O'Neil (Acme, Platform)

Summary: Technical deep dive on guardrails and moderation placement. Focus on performance impact (latency/throughput), KV cache and batching interactions, quantization effects on safety classifiers, and VPC/on-prem deployment options for moderation to meet compliance.

[00:00] Samir: All right everybody, thanks for joining. The goal today is to walk through guardrail placement options and understand the perf impact so we can design the pilot. We'll cover inline moderation, async pipelines, where to attach safety checks to the generation flow, and how that interacts with KV cache and batching. Ava will lead the perf specifics.

[00:27] Ava: Quick agenda—1) baseline numbers for generation without moderation, 2) classifier/moderation options and expected overhead, 3) batching/KV cache interactions, 4) quantization and model-size effects, 5) VPC/on-prem considerations, 6) open Q&A.

[00:45] Carlos: Great. For context, our main consumer is a chat-assistant that serves financial advice to customers. Latency SLO is 300ms p50 on simple queries, p90 can go to 700ms but we want to avoid any large spikes. Throughput target initially is 100 RPS. Data residency and audit logs are required.

[01:10] Priya: From security side, we need indelible audit trails, and ideally moderation should be auditable and deterministic. We also must consider that some data cannot leave our VPC for compliance reasons.

[01:28] Ava: Noted. Baseline: on our hosted runtime with a medium-sized LLM (approx 7B quantized to int8) and continuous batching tuned for conversational traffic, we typically see around 80–120ms per request median for short responses (<=200 tokens) with ~100 RPS using dedicated capacity. p90 is around 240–320ms depending on sequence length. That baseline is without any external safety classifier.

[02:12] Liam: When you say continuous batching, what's the batch latency tradeoff? We're worried about batching adding to p50.

[02:22] Ava: Continuous batching introduces micro-batching delays — we add a configurable window, usually 10–20ms default. For our latency-sensitive configs we push it to 5–10ms but that reduces throughput slightly. So batching itself is not the biggest overhead; the moderation classifier is.

[02:50] Samir: Let's talk classifier placement—three high-level options: 1) pre-filter before generation (quick classifier on prompt only), 2) inline synchronous classifier during/after generation (run on the finished output), 3) async post-processing pipeline (produce response, deliver to user, then moderate and take remediation actions). Each has tradeoffs.

[03:20] Ava: Pre-filter is cheapest latency-wise if the classifier is a small model run on CPU or a tiny GPU. It avoids wasted generation compute for obviously disallowed prompts. But it's blind to hallucinations/misleading outputs because it only sees the prompt. So it reduces some risk but not all. Typical added latency for a small pre-filter is 10–30ms if run on a dedicated CPU service, or 5–15ms if colocated on the same GPU node with an optimized kernel.

[03:58] Priya: That 10–30ms—does it scale with token length?

[04:04] Ava: Pre-filter on the prompt scales with prompt length but prompts are generally short. The bigger concern is the classifier model size and whether it's batched. A small BERT-ish classifier on CPU is tokenization + forward pass; tokenization ~2–8ms, forward pass ~5–20ms depending on quantization and hardware.

[04:30] Carlos: What about inline synchronous moderation that checks the generated text? That seems like it gives the most accurate safety signal.

[04:39] Ava: Correct—inline post-generation check gives you visibility into output content and can block or redact before sending. But it couples moderation latency to user-perceived latency. A moderately sized classifier on GPU might add 40–120ms depending on batching. On CPU it's often higher and can become a bottleneck at scale.

[05:05] Liam: Do you support running the classifier in the same process as the generator so it can reuse tokenizer/KV cache?

[05:13] Ava: We have two deployment patterns: colocated models (same GPU node) or sidecar services (separate process/machine). Colocated can save some tokenizer overhead if both use same tokenizer and we reuse tokenization output, and it can slightly reduce inter-process comms, maybe shaving 5–15ms. But colocating consumes GPU memory and can reduce capacity for generation. Sidecar allows independent scaling of moderation models.

[05:44] Samir: Another idea is to run a tiny fast classifier synchronously and a heavier classifier asynchronously. So the sync one does a quick high-recall check and blocks obvious cases; the async one performs deeper analysis and remediation (like reporting or escalation).

[06:02] Carlos: That seems appealing. How well does that hybrid pattern reduce user-facing latency?

[06:09] Ava: Typically the fast sync filter adds ~10–30ms; you catch most gross violations. The async heavier model can be batched heavily and run off the request path, so it doesn't affect latency but still gives you audit and remediation. For throughput, async processing is more efficient because you can batch thousands of items, lowering per-item CPU/GPU cost.

[06:33] Priya: Does async moderation cause user trust issues if something is delivered and later removed? We need deterministic rules for remediation and clear audit trails.

[06:46] Samir: Good point—remediation policies should be defined up-front. Options include immediate rollback (if severe), notifying the user and retracting, or flagging for human review. The customer can choose a policy depending on risk profile. Also we can keep immutable audit logs and store originals for investigation.

[07:08] Ava: Let's quantify overhead numbers we typically see in production: a small CPU classifier (quantized) — extra 15–40ms; a medium GPU classifier — 40–120ms; a heavy multimodal safety model — 150–400ms if synchronous. Async batch runs reduce effective per-item compute significantly (10–50ms equivalent when amortized), but adds time to detection.

[07:35] Carlos: How does KV cache interact with this? If we run pre-filter then generate, we're good. But if inline moderation requires token-level inspection mid-generation, does KV cache help or hurt?

[07:49] Ava: KV cache primarily speeds up autoregressive generation by caching past key/values per token. It doesn't help the moderation classifier unless the classifier reuses tokenized representations or the model architecture is shared. If you integrate a classifier into the same model, you can potentially reuse hidden states for detection with near-zero extra latency—this is architecture-specific and more complex.

[08:17] Liam: Reusing hidden states sounds interesting but risky. Does Redwood support hooking safety heads into the generative model?

[08:25] Ava: We have a roadmap for model-fusion where a lightweight safety head runs on top of generator hidden states to detect unsafe content earlier. That saves compute but requires changes to model weights or a custom serving wrapper. For now, most customers use separate classifiers or a two-model approach.

[08:45] Priya: What about streaming? For UX reasons we stream tokens to the client. How do we moderate streaming outputs? If inline synchronous classifiers run only after generation, users will already have seen content.

[08:59] Ava: Streaming complicates things. Options: 1) buffer until moderation completes then stream, 2) stream immediately and implement client-side redaction/notice on remediation, 3) use lightweight safety checks that can run incrementally as the stream produces tokens and stop the stream early if flagged. Incremental safety checks usually have lower per-segment overhead but higher complexity.

[09:28] Carlos: Is incremental checking compatible with batching?

[09:33] Ava: It's harder. Batching favors full-request throughput; incremental checks need to analyze partial outputs and are often executed per-stream event, which reduces batching opportunities and can increase overall compute. There's a tradeoff between latency fairness for streaming vs absolute throughput.

[09:54] Samir: Another axis—where moderation runs relative to the customer's control plane. For regulated industries you may want moderation inside the customer's VPC or entirely on-prem. That reduces data egress concerns but moves compute responsibility to the customer. Redwood supports VPC-hosted private deployments for that use-case.

[10:14] Priya: If we run moderation inside our VPC, can we use Redwood's models or do we need to bring our own classifier?

[10:21] Ava: Both are possible. We offer a deployable moderation package that runs in the VPC. Alternatively, customers can bring their own classifier and integrate into our routing. Bring-your-own gives full control over models/weights but we need to validate integration and provide SDK hooks.

[10:39] Carlos: How does quantization affect classifier accuracy? We plan to quantize to reduce footprint.

[10:45] Ava: Quantization can slightly degrade classifier accuracy depending on techniques and calibration. For many classifiers quantized to int8 the loss is minimal (<1–3% relative accuracy drop) if you use quant-aware training or post-training calibration. For aggressive 4-bit quantization, you may see larger drops—worth testing. We recommend running accuracy/regression tests on your prompt sets.

[11:09] Liam: Do we see big differences in latency for quantized classifiers?

[11:14] Ava: Yes—quantized models run faster and use less memory. A quantized int8 CPU inference can be 1.5–3x faster than FP32 on the same hardware for small models. On GPU, 8-bit kernels also reduce runtime and memory, and 4-bit can improve throughput but requires specialized kernels. So quantization helps both latency and cost.

[11:36] Samir: Let's discuss throughput implications and cost. If you run synchronous GPU-based moderation for every request at 100 RPS, you'll need enough GPU capacity to serve both generator and classifier. Sidecars let you scale classifier instances independently and use cheaper CPU-based classifiers for the quick sync pass.

[11:56] Ava: Example cost/throughput case—100 RPS with synchronous medium classifier on GPU might need 1–2 additional GPU nodes dedicated to classification depending on model size. If you switch to a two-tier approach (fast CPU sync + async heavy GPU batch), you can reduce GPU spend significantly and still catch most cases quickly.

[12:20] Priya: For auditing we need logged decisions with context and hashes so we can replay. Does Redwood provide hooks for immutable audit logs?

[12:28] Samir: Yes we provide audit logs, request/response snapshots, and can store classification decisions and model versions. For VPC/on-prem, logs stay inside the customer's storage. We also have integrations with SIEM systems.

[12:43] Carlos: A practical question—we'd like to measure the user-perceived latency hit if we move from no moderation to a fast pre-filter vs inline. What metrics should we collect in the benchmark?

[12:53] Ava: Collect p50/p90/p99 latency for end-to-end response, classifier latency distributions, CPU/GPU utilization, throughput achieved vs target, number of items caught by pre-filter vs final classifier, batching efficiency (average batch size), and token-level cost. Also measure false positive/false negative rates on labeled prompt sets.

[13:17] Liam: How should we simulate real traffic? Bursty vs steady?

[13:21] Ava: Both. Run steady-state tests to measure throughput and tail latencies, and burst tests to see how fallback policies behave (e.g., queueing, degraded quality, switching to cheaper models). Include streaming scenarios if you stream to clients.

[13:36] Priya: One more compliance question—if moderation runs async and is hosted by Redwood, is there any window where sensitive content could be exposed? We need to quantify risk and retention policies.

[13:48] Samir: If Redwood-hosted async moderation is used, there will be a time delta between delivery and detection. We can minimize retention and ensure encryption at rest and transit; also provide options to store only hashes and metadata instead of full text. For the highest compliance, VPC/on-prem is recommended.

[14:08] Carlos: On implementation—can you show us where to plug a custom classifier into Redwood's routing?

[14:14] Ava: Yes, we have an SDK endpoint and a sidecar pattern. In the demo docs we show how to route requests to a custom webhook for pre-filtering, or register a sidecar service for inline checks. I'll drop links after the call.

[14:28] Samir: Let's cover a few example architectures that came up: A) Quick sync CPU pre-filter + generator on GPU + async GPU heavy filter for post-hoc audits. B) Colocated generator + safety-head using hidden states (requires model changes). C) VPC-hosted full stack where customer runs both generator and classifier for compliance. D) Streaming incremental checks with client-side redaction.

[14:57] Carlos: Which is most recommended for a financial use-case wanting low latency and strong auditability?

[15:03] Ava: For financial with strict compliance, we often recommend A or C. A gives a good balance—fast sync filter reduces obvious events, async heavy checks give auditability. C if customer wants full control over data residency and doesn't mind running infrastructure.

[15:22] Priya: Any gotchas re: KV cache and async pipelines? If we run async remediation and then need to re-generate with safer constraints, how do we ensure the same cache state so outputs are reproducible?

[15:36] Ava: Reproducibility is tricky. KV cache depends on prior conversation state. If you need to re-generate a safer response, you should snapshot the conversation state (keys/values) or re-run generation deterministically (seed + same model version). We usually recommend capturing conversation context and a hash so you can replay.

[15:55] Liam: For the benchmark plan, what concrete steps did we agree on?

[16:00] Samir: Ava will run benchmarks: baseline (no moderation), pre-filter sync (CPU), inline sync (GPU), async heavy (batched). Use 100 RPS steady and a burst test to 300 RPS. Use the 10 prompt sets Carlos will provide. We'll measure latencies, batch sizes, resource utilization, and detection rates.

[16:20] Carlos: We'll prepare the prompt sets and share them by Wednesday.

[16:24] Priya: We'll also decide whether to require VPC for pilot by Tuesday; if so we need deployment steps.

[16:30] Samir: Next steps recap—Ava benchmarks, Samir sends docs, Carlos & Priya provide prompts and compliance constraints. We'll reconvene to review results.

[16:38] Ava: Quick Q&A—Carlos: you asked earlier about model-fusion safety heads. It's a higher-effort integration but can yield near-zero extra latency. Worth exploring in longer term.

[16:52] Carlos: Thanks—sounds good. One risk: false positives on financial terminology. We'll need a whitelist or fine-tuning.

[17:00] Ava: Absolutely. We recommend fine-tuning or custom thresholding and maintaining an allowlist for domain-specific terms. That also factors into classifier calibration in the benchmark.

[17:14] Priya: For audit logs, please include model version and classifier thresholds in the log so we can correlate decisions.

[17:22] Samir: Will do. We'll include model version, hash, thresholds, and the raw or hashed content depending on your retention config.

[17:34] Liam: Any notes on failures—if classifier service is down, fallback behaviors?

[17:41] Ava: Yes, Redwood supports configurable fallback: 1) fail closed (block), 2) fail open (deliver and flag), 3) route to cheaper classifier or reduced QPS. Customers should pick based on risk tolerance. We'll capture that in the pilot config.

[17:58] Samir: Okay, wrapping up. Thanks everybody. We'll share the benchmark plan and docs.

[18:08] Carlos: Thanks all. Looking forward to seeing the numbers.

[18:12] Priya: Thanks. We'll coordinate internally and get you those prompts.

[18:15] Samir: End notes—links I'll share: Redwood moderation architecture doc (https://redwood.example.com/docs/moderation-arch), safety tuning guide (https://redwood.example.com/docs/safety-tuning), SOC2 summary (https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2).

[18:30] Meeting end.
